title: Reading Results Like a Detective: The Low Anion Gap and Protein Effects
summary: Use the anion gap’s dependence on albumin to recognize when a very low or negative gap is a clue — laboratory error, bromism or a paraprotein — and why measured ionized calcium beats a calculated corrected calcium.

reviewer.note: Teaches Ch. 9 Hits 2–3 and Traps 2 and 5 (first lesson for Ch. 9). Checked against Wartak 2012, Laakman 2022, Desgagnés 2025 and Mirrakhimov 2015. Discrepancies already in the register: the “≈ 12 (8–16)” normal anion gap (rv-ag-normal, method-dependent) and the 4.4 g/dL reference albumin (rv-calcium-ref-albumin; open sources use 4.0). Not taught here (covered by other lessons or not yet sourced): IDA vs ACD, BUN/creatinine ratio, diabetes cut-offs, troponin kinetics, heparin/warfarin tests, mixing study, cortisol/ACTH patterns, COPD oxygen, DIC, lipase vs amylase, fulminant hepatic failure.

objectives: Explain what the anion gap represents and how albumin affects it.
List the causes of a very low or negative anion gap and the first step when one is found.
Explain why measured ionized calcium is preferred to albumin-corrected calcium.

scenes.title: An anion gap of zero
scenes.altText: Case adapted from a published report (Wartak 2012): a 50-year-old with anaemia, bone pain and confusion has (illustrative values) Na 138, Cl 110, HCO₃⁻ 28 mmol/L — anion gap 0 (his outpatient gap had been 3–4). Albumin 2.0 g/dL; total protein 12.6 g/dL. Total calcium is reported with a “corrected” value. Question token: “Is a zero anion gap just a quirk of low albumin — and what does it hint at?”

cues.text: A 50-year-old with anaemia, bone pain and confusion has an anion gap of zero. His gap had been 3 to 4 in clinic.
His albumin is low, 2 grams per decilitre, but his total protein is very high: 12.6.
Is a zero gap just low albumin, or is it a clue? And can his corrected calcium be trusted?

props.label: Quirk of low albumin — or a clue?

scenes.title: Where the anion gap comes from
scenes.altText: Gap card (Wartak 2012): AG = Na⁺ − (Cl⁻ + HCO₃⁻); the gap exists because unmeasured anions exceed unmeasured cations, and normally most of it is the negative charge on circulating proteins, mainly ALBUMIN. Range card (Wartak 2012, citing population studies with contemporary electrolyte measurement): normal AG about 6–10 mmol/L; it is method-dependent — use your laboratory’s range (see register rv-ag-normal). Worked arithmetic for the hook: 138 − (110 + 28) = 0.

cues.text: The anion gap is sodium minus chloride plus bicarbonate. It is not a real gap: it reflects anions we do not routinely measure.
Most of those unmeasured anions are negative charges on proteins, above all albumin.
With modern electrolyte methods, studies put the normal gap at roughly 6 to 10, but each laboratory should use its own range.
For our patient: 138 minus 110 plus 28 gives zero. Something has removed the usual anions, or added unmeasured cations.

scenes.title: What can push the gap down
scenes.altText: Albumin card (Wartak 2012): for each 1 g/dL fall in albumin, the AG falls by about 2.5 mmol/L — so albumin 2.0 g/dL explains only part of a drop, not a gap of zero. Causes card (Laakman 2022, review of 2.9 million specimens and the literature): negative or very low gaps arise from LABORATORY ERROR, specimen contamination or interference, hypoalbuminaemia, extreme hyperkalaemia, BROMISM, and PARAPROTEINS from multiple myeloma or similar disorders. Wartak 2012: severe bromide, iodide or lithium intoxication can lower the AG; rises in unmeasured cations (K⁺, Ca²⁺, Mg²⁺) usually have little effect.

cues.text: Low albumin lowers the gap: about 2.5 units for every 1 gram per decilitre lost. But that explains only part of a drop to zero.

In a review of nearly three million specimens and the literature, the causes of very low or negative gaps were laboratory error, contamination or interference, low albumin, extreme hyperkalaemia, bromide poisoning, and paraproteins.
Severe bromide, iodide or lithium poisoning can also lower the gap, so the drug history matters.
And a large paraprotein, as in myeloma, can drive the gap down to zero or below. So first repeat the test to exclude error, then look for these causes.

props.label: Repeat first → then look for causes

scenes.title: Proteins and calcium
scenes.altText: Resolution card (Wartak 2012): the repeat AG remained 0 to −1; serum protein 12.6 g/dL and gamma globulin 7.5 g/dL; immunofixation showed an IgG-κ monoclonal protein; marrow 70% plasma cells — multiple myeloma. Calcium card (Desgagnés 2025; Mirrakhimov 2015): albumin-adjusted (“corrected”) calcium uses the simplified Payne formula — Ca (mmol/L) + 0.02 × (40 − albumin g/L), equivalent to Ca (mg/dL) + 0.8 × (4.0 − albumin g/dL); in a large study, unadjusted total calcium correlated with IONIZED calcium better than the adjusted value; ionized calcium may be preferred when albumin is abnormal. Hook answers: a zero gap is a clue — repeat, then look for a paraprotein; measure ionized calcium rather than trusting a corrected value.

cues.text: In the published case, the repeat gap was still zero to minus one. Immunofixation found an IgG kappa monoclonal protein, and the marrow was 70 percent plasma cells: myeloma.
Proteins distort calcium too. Corrected calcium adds 0.8 milligrams per decilitre for each gram of albumin below 4.0.
But in a large study, uncorrected total calcium matched ionized calcium better than the corrected value did. When albumin is abnormal, measure ionized calcium.
So the zero gap was a clue, not a quirk: repeat it, then search for a paraprotein. And for calcium, trust a measured ionized value over a calculated correction.

props.label: Hook: zero AG = clue → paraprotein · measure ionized Ca

scenes.title: Three classic traps
scenes.altText: Three trap cards: “A gap of 2 is fine because it’s low” (✓ a very low or negative gap needs a repeat and a search for error, bromism or a paraprotein); “Low albumin explains any low gap” (✓ ≈ 2.5 mmol/L per 1 g/dL — it rarely explains a gap of zero); “A corrected calcium is as good as ionized calcium” (✓ unadjusted total correlated better with ionized calcium in a large study; measure ionized calcium when albumin is abnormal).

cues.text: Trap one: a gap of 2 is fine because it is low. No: a very low gap needs a repeat, then a search for error, bromide or a paraprotein.
Trap two: low albumin explains any low gap. No: it lowers the gap about 2.5 for each gram per decilitre, rarely enough to reach zero.
Trap three: corrected calcium is as good as ionized calcium. No: in a large study the correction performed worse. Measure ionized calcium.

scenes.title: The missing negative charge
scenes.altText: Memory aid: “The gap is mostly ALBUMIN’S NEGATIVE CHARGE. Lose albumin and the gap shrinks a little; add a big paraprotein and it can vanish. If the gap hits zero, think: Error, Bromide, or a Big Band (paraprotein).” Tokens: albumin −2.5/g · zero gap → E-B-B · ionized Ca > corrected. A card lists where the aid breaks.

cues.text: Memory aid: the gap is mostly albumin’s negative charge. Lose albumin and it shrinks a little; add a large paraprotein and it can vanish. If the gap hits zero, think error, bromide, or a big band.
Where it breaks: not every paraprotein lowers the gap, so a normal gap does not exclude one; normal ranges depend on the electrolyte method; and correction formulas vary between laboratories.

props.title: Where it breaks

scenes.title: Takeaway
scenes.altText: Two tokens: “AG = Na − (Cl + HCO₃) · mostly albumin · −2.5 per 1 g/dL albumin · very low/negative → repeat, then error, bromism, extreme K⁺, paraprotein”, “Corrected calcium is unreliable — measure ionized calcium”.

cues.text: Because the anion gap is mostly albumin’s negative charge, low albumin lowers it modestly, so a gap near zero should be repeated and then investigated for error, bromism or a paraprotein, and calcium status is best judged by measured ionized calcium.

props.label: AG mostly albumin · −2.5/g · ≈ 0 → repeat → error, bromide, paraprotein
Corrected calcium unreliable → measure ionized calcium

explanation.what: Plain language: the anion gap is a bookkeeping difference that mostly reflects the negative charge on albumin; when it is unexpectedly near zero, something unusual — a lab mistake, a poison such as bromide, or a large abnormal antibody protein — may be present. Scientific terms: anion gap, unmeasured anions/cations, hypoalbuminaemia, bromism, paraprotein, immunofixation, multiple myeloma, albumin-adjusted (corrected) calcium, ionized calcium.
explanation.why: Albumin carries most of the unmeasured negative charge, so losing it lowers the gap; large amounts of certain paraproteins, or substances that interfere with chloride measurement, push it further. Calcium binds albumin, but correction formulas approximate this poorly, so a direct ionized measurement is more reliable.
explanation.measure: AG = Na⁺ − (Cl⁻ + HCO₃⁻); normal ≈ 6–10 with contemporary methods (method-dependent); −2.5 per 1 g/dL fall in albumin (Wartak 2012). Very low/negative AG: repeat, then consider error, contamination/interference, hypoalbuminaemia, extreme hyperkalaemia, bromism, paraprotein (Laakman 2022). Corrected Ca (mg/dL) = Ca + 0.8 × (4.0 − albumin); ionized Ca preferred (Desgagnés 2025; Mirrakhimov 2015).
explanation.differs: Hypoalbuminaemia (modest, predictable fall in AG) vs paraprotein or bromism (larger, unexpected fall); calculated corrected calcium vs measured ionized calcium.
explanation.examAngle: Expect: calculate an anion gap, recognize that a very low gap is abnormal and points to myeloma or bromism after excluding error, and choose ionized calcium in hypoalbuminaemia.

questions.stem: Na 140, Cl 112, HCO₃⁻ 27 mmol/L. What is the anion gap?

options.rationale: Incorrect. Subtract both chloride and bicarbonate from sodium.
Incorrect. That is Na − Cl only.

questions.stem: A patient’s anion gap is −1 on repeat testing, albumin is 3.5 g/dL and total protein is markedly raised. What is the most useful next test?

options.rationale: Correct. A negative gap with high protein suggests a paraprotein.
Incorrect. Albumin 3.5 g/dL cannot explain a negative gap.
Incorrect. Lactate raises, not lowers, the gap.

options.text: No further action — a low gap is normal
options.rationale: Incorrect. A negative gap is abnormal.

questions.stem: A patient with albumin 2.0 g/dL has a total calcium of 7.6 mg/dL. What is the best way to assess calcium status?

options.rationale: Correct. Correction formulas are unreliable; ionized calcium is preferred.

options.text: Report a corrected calcium of 9.2 mg/dL as definitive
options.rationale: Incorrect. That uses a 4.0 reference but corrected values agree poorly with ionized calcium.
Incorrect. Repeating total calcium does not address albumin binding.
Incorrect. The gap does not assess calcium status.

accuracyFlags.issue: Ch. 9 Hit 3 repeats the “≈ 12 (8–16)” normal anion gap. With contemporary electrolyte methods the normal gap is lower (about 6–10 in Wartak 2012; see register rv-ag-normal). The range is method-dependent.
Ch. 9 Hit 2 uses reference albumin 4.4 g/dL in the corrected-calcium formula; open sources (Desgagnés 2025; Mirrakhimov 2015) use 4.0 g/dL (register rv-calcium-ref-albumin).
